Methods of investigation Samples for this investigation were collected during 1965-66 by members of a helicopter-supported field party of U.S. Geological Survey geologists. A total of 183 oriented hand samples was collected by A. B. Ford, W. W. Boyd, W. H. Nelson and D. L. Schmidt. Samples were collected during measurement of sections through the entire exposed stratigraphic thickness of the intrusion, and were spaced throughout most of its exposed area. On the assumption that the Dufek intrusion is a gabbroic sheet 6 km in thickness, Fig. 2 of Jaeger (1957) suggests that the time required for the Curie temperature isothermal surface (assumed 500°C) to pass from the margins of the sheet to its centre was on the order of 0.25 My. If the isothermal surface moved at a constant velocity, a stratigraphic thickness of about 0.5m of gabbro anywhere within the sheet should have become magnetized during a period of about 50 years. In this simplified model the isothermal surfaces are assumed to be horizontal, and therefore are roughly parallel to the igneous layering. On the arbitrary assumption that samples which are magnetized less than 50 years apart do not provide independent estimates of the direction of the geomagnetic field, samples sep

nd the remainder of the rock retained for chemical and petrographic studies. Directions of remanent magnetization were measures on a duplicate of the U.S. Geological Survey spinner magnetometer described by Doell & Cox (1965). Certain very weakly magnetized samples were measured on a more sensitive spinner magnetometer designed by Phillips & Kuckes (1967). Magnetic susceptibilities were measured in low magnetic fields by an inductance bridge (Anderson 1961) and checked on a commercial bridge of similar design. y a U.S. Geological Survey expedition. The geology of the intrusion has been described in recent papers by Ford & Boyd (1968, 1969) and Ford (1970). According to these authors the Dufek intrusion is a layered sequence of gabbro and related rock, forming a roughly sheetlike body estimated to be at least 6km thick. Aeromagnetic evidence indicates that the intrusion underlies an area of at least 9500km2 (Behrendt, Meister & Henderson 1966), much of which is covered by ice. Extensive exposures occur in two areas. A thickness of approximately 1.9 km of the stratigraphically lower part of the intrusion, consisting of layered gabbro, anorthosite and pyroxenite, is exposed in the Dufek Massif (Fig. 1). An ice-filled valley about 6Okm wide separates the Dufek Massif rocks from exposures of the upper part of the intrusion, in the Forrestal Range. Forrestal Range rocks have an exposed thickness of approximately 1.6 km, consisting chiefly of a layered gabbro that is more iron rich and more oxidized that the layered gabbro of the Dufek Massif. Granophyre, 0.3km thick, caps the Forrestal Range exposures (Ford 1970). Introduction The basalts of North-east Ireland, covering an area of about 1500 square miles, represent the southernmost part of the Thulean or North Atlantic igneous province. Outlines of the geology have been given by Charlesworth (1953), Walker (1960) and Wilson & Robbie (1966). The Northern Irish lava succession which was extruded subaerially rests in general upon a thin layer of red clay which in turn overlies the eroded surface of the Cretaceous Upper Chalk. The lava sequence is divided into three subsections: the Lower-, the Tholeiitic- and the Upper Basalts. The Lower- and Upper Basalts are olivine basalts with an average olivine content of 15-20 per cent. Prominent lateritic/bauxitic horizons separate the three series from each other, representing interruptions in the volcanic activity of considerable duration. The thinner units of the Lower Basalts have a slaggy and visicular appearance and are often badly altered due to zeolitization and weathering. The Tholeiitic Basalts are fine grained and compact and are distinguished by the virtual absence of olivine and by the presence of glass. The first type of alteration to basaltic rocks following consolidation is the well-known deuteric oxidation process. Simply, this involves the lava rock burning in its own or an acquired gas content. Sat0 & Wright (1966) have followed this process as it happens in cooling contemporary Hawaiian lava lakes-in some parts of the uppermost parts of these lava lakes oxygen fugacity rises dramatically over the 800-500 "C cooling interval; this being accom- panied by reddening of the rock. Changes in the magnetic titanomagnetite during this process have been traced by GrommB, Wright & Peck (1969). The first stage of titano- magnetite deuteric oxidation results in the sub-solidus exsolution of ilmenite lamellae trellises, leaving near pure magnetite as the host. Further oxidation results in the splitting of the ilmenite lamellae into titanohematite and ferri-rutile while finally a pseudomorph consisting of pseudobrookite, titanohematite and rutile completely replaces the original titanomagnetite. Sloan (Received 1971 September 14)t Summary A detailed palaeomagnetic investigation has been made of the Mull (Scotland) regional dyke swarm. 165 dykes were sampled in a 7-km section across the swarm from Quinish to Ardmore in northern Mull. A major question arising from the results of the investigation is whether the cleaned NRM directions for the dykes are equivalent to the original cooling TRM directions. The question arises since evidence from several lines shows that the dykes have experienced considerable hydrothermal alteration, with reheating temperatures averaging 200°C and major changes in the iron titanium oxides responsible for the NRM. Surprisingly, the answer appears to be that original cooling TRM directions are probably still well represented by cleaned NRM directions. Notwithstanding the large number of palaeomagnetic directions obtained from the dykes, no simple picture of the Palaeogene geomagnetic field emerges. Thus, continental drift cannot be estimated from the data. The explanation for the distribution of directions appears to rest between either a short time of activity for the whole

tween either a short time of activity for the whole British Tertiary igneous province with non-representative sampling by the activity in individual areas, or the existence of relatively long periods of non-centred axial dipole behaviour for the geomagnetic field during the Palaeogene. 1. Introduction One uncertainty concerning the basic assumption of palaeomagnetic interpretation dominates this study, that the geomagnetic field direction at the time of initial cooling of a small volcanic unit can be isolated, and much of the paper will be oriented towards answering this doubt. The question that must be asked is whether a series of dykes, probably initially characterized by Curie points largely in the lO(1-200"C temperature interval, can after possibly later reheating to 200°C be made to yield information about the geomagnetic field at the time of initial cooling. If this doubt can be resolved satisfactorily, then consideration can be given to the pattern of geomagnetic field behaviour at the time of the intrusion of the dykes. The sites combine to give a mean direction of D = 3599, I = -3.0" (a95 = 4.4") and the derived palaeomagnetic pole is significantly different from the present pole implying that the field here has not approximated to an axial geocentric dipole in Brunhes epoch times. Thirty-two sites distributed through the volcanic area of Cameroun combine to give a mean direction of D = 4@, I = 4.3" (ag5 = 6.1"). The sites around li4t Cameroun are all normally magnetized and this volcano is believed to have grown in Brunhes epoch times. Analysis of the Upper Tertiary palaeomagnetic results from the African plate demonstrates no detectable movement of the plate relative to the geographic pole for about the past 25 My. 1. Introduction The Gulf of Guinea volcanic province is a linear belt of volcanism that extends more than 300 km across central West Africa from the Bambouto and Manengouba mountains in Cameroun to Mt Cameroun and the island of Fernando Po0 in the Gulf of Guinea (Fig. 1). It continues seawards for a further 700km through the islands of

Fernando Po0 is a youthful island with a topography that is entirely constructional. The northern most volcano (Santa Isabel) lies on the continental shelf and young flows have been emptied from vents on the main fissure zone which is marked by numerous small cinder running along the crest of the volcano (Fig. 5). An eruption was recorded on the south-east slope of this volcano in 1898 and many of the lava flows are evidently very young. The southern two volcanoes (San Carlos, Pic0 Baio) straddle the continental slope and they are covered by many small vents but show no marked linearity. All the rocks on this island are alkali olivine basalt flows often approaching picrites, oceanites, or ankaramites in composition (Fuster Casas 1956). 154 J. D. A. Piper and A. Richardson I I FIG. 6. Geology and palaeomagnetic sampling sites in West Cameroun. 2.6 Cameroun The volcanics of Cameroun belong to three groups (Gkze 1953). The oldest is a series of basalt and andesite flows which ale now heavily laterized but appear to have come from fissure eruptions following the regional SSW-NNE trend and may be Lower Tertiary in age. These rocks cover extensive areas between Mt Cameroun, the Roumpi Mountains and the Manengouba Massif, and occur again in the Bamenda Highlands (Gize 1943).

It continues seawards for a further 700km through the islands of

ian times (76-82My). Sedi- mentation in the Cameroun area continued uninterrupted to lower Eocene times, after which there is a gap in the stratigraphic record which appears to coincide with the development of the Massif of Adamaoua as a faulted monoclinal margin to the Benue rift. The faulting and uplift of this massif coincides with the first phase of volcanism in the Bamenda Highlands of Cameroun (GQe 1953) but volcanism did not commence in the Mt Cameroun area until middle Miocene to early Pliocene times (Hedburg 1968). The volcanic islands are distinctly oceanic in chemical character and are formed principally of alkali olivine basalts and basic accumulates; the lavas are commonly intruded on the islands of Principe, S5o Tomt and Annobon by domes of trachyte, phonolite and tephrite. Mt Cameroun is a basaltic shield volcano which is morpho- logically and chemically similar to the volcanoes of Fernando Poo, but north-eastwards along the lineament rocks of calc-alkaline affinities become more important. Andesites, peralkaline trachytes and rhyolites are found in the Bambouto, Roumpi and Maenengouba mountains (Gkze 1943, 1953; Jeremine 1941, 1943). Fernando Po0 is a youthful island with a topography that is entirely constructional. The northern most volcano (Santa Isabel) lies on the continental shelf and young flows have been emptied from vents on the main fissure zone which is marked by numerous small cinder running along the crest of the volcano (Fig. 5). An eruption was recorded on the south-east slope of this volcano in 1898 and many of the lava flows are evidently very young. The southern two volcanoes (San Carlos, Pic0 Baio) straddle the continental slope and they are covered by many small vents but show no marked linearity. The island of Annobon is built up of a suite of reversely magnetized lavas about 18.4 My in age which give a mean direction of D = 189-2", I = 11.2" (N = 7, a95 = 153"). A younger phase of volcanism dated as 2.6My has produced lavas with a mean direction of magnetization of D = 337-1", I = -44.3" (N = 7, ag5 = 9.3"). The accessible parts of the island of SHo Tom6 are covered by young lavas of Pliocene and younger age with both polarities. The Girnar hills in Kathiawar peninsula of Gujarat, India form a part of the Deccan trap formation of peninsular India. This impressive formation is very similar to the Columbia basalts in U.S.A. and Sera Geral formation in south America. The traps at present cover approximately an area of 200 OOO sq. miles extending from nearly 69.5" to 82" E and 16" to 23" N. The present distribution shows that the traps could have covered originally a much larger area, of the order of 500OOOsq. miles including a large segment which now forms a part of the Arabian Sea to the west of Bombay. Palaeomagnetically this is one of the most widely studied formations of the world. Several investigators have contributed to the study of the Deccan traps. The south-west and middle-west areas have been studied by Hospers (1951, 1953 and 1954), Sigurgeirsson (1957), Brynjolfsson (1956, 1957), Einarsson (1957a, b), Einarsson & Sigurgeirsson (1955), and most recently by Piper (1971). Field procedure A minimum of four cores were taken from each of 80 sites in the Foyers Plutonic Complex, and its associated country rocks. Cores, 5-8 cm long, were drilled using a portable two-stroke petrol motor, and oriented, in situ, relative to the Sun, or a known distant geographical feature. Eighty-six per cent of the cores were Sun- sighted. 4. Palaeomagnetic results The oriented cores were sliced into 2.5-cm specimens for the purpose of measuring their remanent directions. The N.R.M. of each specimen was measured using a parastatic magnetometer. Stepwise a/c demagnetization was then carried out at 50-0e intervals, up to a maximum of 1400 Oe; and the remanence of each specimen measured after each demagnetization step. The parastatic magnetometer is linked to a computer, which calculates the direction of magnetization immediately after each measurement, thus enabling the changes in direction to be plotted immediately. The demagnetization process was continued until a stable direction was attained. Twenty-three sites gave stable directions of magnetization. Whatever their origin, the mean VGP for each period are clearly significantly different from the geographic pole (Figs 10 and 11). Perhaps more surprising is the almost identical positions of the VGP (Table 3). Because of the unique large volume and age control of the constituent data, this coincidence of VGP for the three geological periods must be considered to be probably realistic. The favoured interpretation of these results is the systematic long-period distortion of the geomagnetic field, by either an offset dipole or by an unequal co-axial dipole pair, as discussed above. This is much more feasible than a simple polar wandering model, since it would be necessary to invoke a greater than 5" per million years polar wandering rate, for the past 1.6 My to explain the results. Gronim6 & Vine (1972) believe that no true polar wander has occured since at least t = 17 My. These latter two publications, together with the work of Watkins & Abdel- Monem (1971) provide fine details of stratigraphic horizons and sample sites for all the units which were subject to K:Ar analyses. Whatever their origin, the mean VGP for each period are clearly significantly different from the geographic pole (Figs 10 and 11). Perhaps more surprising is the almost identical positions of the VGP (Table 3). Because of the unique large volume and age control of the constituent data, this coincidence of VGP for the three geological periods must be considered to be probably realistic. The favoured interpretation of these results is the systematic long-period distortion of the geomagnetic field, by either an offset dipole or by an unequal co-axial dipole pair, as discussed above. This is much more feasible than a simple polar wandering model, since it would be necessary to invoke a greater than 5" per million years polar wandering rate, for the past 1.6 My to explain the results. Gronim6 & Vine (1972) believe that no true polar wander has occured since at least t = 17 My. When the confidence limits are added to the mean VGP (Table 3, Fig. 11) no conclusions can be made concerning the polar wandering rate from the Pleistocene to the Miocene periods. There is currently considerable dispute as to whether the TRM of multidomain grains resides in restricted regions displaying properties expected of single domains (Verhoogen 1959) or whether it can be satisfactorily accounted for by multidomain theory (Stacey 1963). The magnetic properties of the Obuasi greenstone suggests that the remanence is dominated by multidomain carriers, and petrographic observa- tion shows that these must be unoxidized magnetite. This is associated with ilmenite as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low temperature metasomatic origin. Crystallizing slowly under such conditions the magnetite may owe its small and unstable TRM to the absence of dislocations in the crystal lattice (Verhoogen 1959). 4.2. There is currently considerable dispute as to whether the TRM of multidomain grains resides in restricted regions displaying properties expected of single domains (Verhoogen 1959) or whether it can be satisfactorily accounted for by multidomain theory (Stacey 1963). The magnetic properties of the Obuasi greenstone suggests that the remanence is dominated by multidomain carriers, and petrographic observa- tion shows that these must be unoxidized magnetite. This is associated with ilmenite as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low temperature metasomatic origin. Crystallizing slowly under such conditions the magnetite may owe its small and unstable TRM to the absence of dislocations in the crystal lattice (Verhoogen 1959). 4.2. There is currently considerable dispute as to whether the TRM of multidomain grains resides in restricted regions displaying properties expected of single domains (Verhoogen 1959) or whether it can be satisfactorily accounted for by multidomain theory (Stacey 1963). The magnetic properties of the Obuasi greenstone suggests that the remanence is dominated by multidomain carriers, and petrographic observa- tion shows that these must be unoxidized magnetite. This is associated with ilmenite as a separate phase and the mineralogy of the rock demonstrates that it has a low temperature metasomatic origin. Crystallizing slowly under such conditions the magnetite may owe its small and unstable TRM to the absence of dislocations in the crystal lattice (Verhoogen 1959). 4.2. All the members defined by Jones & Pugh (1949) were sampled except the basal Fine Ash and Shales, and the Red Agglomerate and Ash. The pole position in Ordovician times There are several lines of evidence to suggest that the mean NRM directions of the two suites of rocks studied are indicative of the local Ordovician geomagnetic field. Principally the remanences are pre-tilting because their in situ directions do not match the inferred local geomagnetic field direction at any subsequent time. Introduction The basic intrusions of north-east Scotland form a major igneous province and consist of several large and many small intrusions of predominantly gabbroic composition. The outcrop covers an area of some 2500km2, and the larger bodies are the Huntly, Insch, Haddo House, Arnage, Maud and Belhelvie masses (Fig. 1). They predate the post-orogenic granites of the area and appear to have been intruded at about the climax of Caledonian regional metamorphism. They have been divided by Read (1919) into two suites: an ' Older ' suite of amphibolitized and foliated bodies and a ' Younger ' unmetamorphosed suite. The Younger suite, which forms the subject of the present paper, has been extensively examined by Read (1923, 1935, 1955, 1956), Read & Farquhar (1952, 1956) and Stewart (1946), but their interpretation of structural relationships has been a matter of controversy. Vertical rhythmic banding occurs in the Belhelvie mass and steeply dipping bands occur in the Huntly and Insch masses. T

Notably all well established palaeomagnetic poles from British Devonian rocks lie well to the west of contemporary poles derived from Norway and Russia. The Biitish data comprise results from the Midland Valley lavas (Stubbs 1958; Embleton 1968; McMurry 1968, 1970), the flat lying Old Red Sandstone sediments of the Anglo-Welsh cuvette (Chamalaun & Creer 1964) and intrusive rocks of ‘Lower Old Red Sandstone age ’ in the south-west highlands of Scotland (Briden 1970). Chamalaun & Creer (1964) showed that, apart from a minor high critical blocking temperature component revealed during thermal demagnetization, the NRM in the Anglo-Welsh Old Red Sandstone sediments is largely secondary, and unrelated to the Devonian magnetic field. This study was undertaken to establish details of the British palaeomagnetic record using the detailed stratigraphic information derived from recent mapping by the Institute of Geological Sciences (Armstrong & Paterson 1970). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: one of several concerning Devonian palaeomagnetic results throughout Europe, reviewed in Paper VI. Notably all well established palaeomagnetic poles from British Devonian rocks lie well to the west of contemporary poles derived from Norway and Russia. The Biitish data comprise results from the Midland Valley lavas (Stubbs 1958; Embleton 1968; McMurry 1968, 1970), the flat lying Old Red Sandstone sediments of the Anglo-Welsh cuvette (Chamalaun & Creer 1964) and intrusive rocks of ‘Lower Old Red Sandstone age ’ in the south-west highlands of Scotland (Briden 1970). Chamalaun & Creer (1964) showed that, apart from a minor high critical blocking temperature component revealed during thermal demagnetization, the NRM in the Anglo-Welsh Old Red Sandstone sediments is largely secondary, and unrelated to the Devonian magnetic field. This study was undertaken to establish details of the British palaeomagnetic record using the detailed stratigraphic information derived from recent mapping by the Institute of Geological Sciences (Armstrong & Paterson 1970). This metamorphism is superimposed upon the Dalradian regional metamorphism and its mineralogical effect was principally to increase grainsize. If the iron oxides participated in this crystal growth, formerly small superparamagnetic grains may have been transposed into the ferromagnetic domain size region explaining the susceptibility variation. The principal finding from thermal demagnetization, as described below, is that even the outermost samples, 170m from the contact, appear to carry a total TRM in magnetite. Hence total intensity variation across the aureole must reflect these detailed changes in the magnetic mineralogy throughout the remanence-bearing phase, and not merely in the very low coercivity region which is reflected in measure- ments of x. The stability of natural remanence (NRM) against progressive thermal demagneti- zation (Figs 3 and 4) changes abruptly near 25 m from the contact, which is regarded as the divide between ' inner ' and ' outer ' parts of the aureole. This division is apparent in progressive AF demagnetization of typical specimens (Briden 1970), and in the generalized AF properties of the two zones given in Fi

er aureole. The main remanence carrier exhibits different spectra of coercivities (below 550 Oe) and blocking temperatures (below 570 "C) in the inner and outer zones. These spectra can be matched in the two zones to produce the cor- relation between critical blocking temperature and remanence coercivity illustrated in Fig. 4(c). Up to about 500°C a linear relationship appears to hold, but at higher temperatures the coercivity dependence is more sensitive. The relation TB c1 log H,, empirically describes the whole range of observations in Fig. 4(c). It is notable that the maximum TB and HCR correspond to the maximum observed values in magnetite or Ti-poor titanomagnetite. Petrological investigation confirms that this ' magnetite ' is the commonest opaque phase throughout, and it is therefore likely to be the principal carrier of remanence. In the light of this situation another approach to the problem of relating the ages of the central intrusive complexes, the dykes that cut these complexes and the linear dyke swarm is justified. Palaeomagnetism may offer such an approach. Both the Mull linear dyke swarm, sampled along the north coast of Mull, and the plateau basalts of the Gribun-Ben More area contain both normal and reverse polarities, with the sequence in both cases being: R -+ N -+ R from oldest to youngest (Ade-Hall et al. 1972; Ade-Hall, Dagley & Wilson 1974). In the lavas the polarity sequence has been obtained by a comparison of remanence polarities with the stratigraphic order of flows. The average diameter of the ring dyke is close to 10 km and the block of lavas and other intrusives enclosed within it can be shown to have subsided by at least 1 km. The only components of the Tertiary volcanic episode of north-west Britain known to be younger than the ring dyke are the small number of north-west trending basic dykes which cut the ring dyke. The temporal relationship of these dykes to the Mull linear dyke swarm as a whole and thus of the latter to the central intrusive complexes are questions of interest. The dykes cutting the Loch BA felsite ring dyke are petrologically similar, and have similar NW to NNW strikes to the Mull dyke swarm, which, while focussed on the Mull intrusive centres, extends for at least 600 km from the Outer Hebrides Islands (58" 30' N, 352" 30' E) to Yorkshire (54" 30' N, 359" 30' E). For these reasons the dykes cutting the Loch BA felsite and those of the Mull linear swarm have long been supposed to be co-eval. From radiometric dating studies it seems most probable that the whole period of this Tertiary volcanic activity was only a few million years in duration, with a median age of close to 59 My (Macintyre 1973). With the usual 5 per cent or greater magnitude of analytical and other errors involved in radiometric dating, this means that the ages of individual units of the activity cannot be resolved. The conclusion probably holds in spite of a wide range of apparent ages for volcanic material from Mull. Thus, Mussett et al. These can apparently be related to the geological history of the rocks or their mode of surface occurrence. Throughout an entire rock formation, rocks can acquire a stable ancient secondary magnetization by internal processes (e.g. Briden 1965, 1967; Chamalaun 1964; Farrell & May 1969; Ku et al. 1967; Irving & Opdyke 1965; Storetvedt 1968). Rocks on, or close to, the surface can acquire secondary magnetizations due to surface effects (Irving 1964), whereas samples recovered from a road cut do not (e.g. Graham & Hales 1961). In this article surface samples refer to rock samples collected from natural exposures and not from recent deep road cuts. Palaeomagnetists want to avoid the problems of surface effects on samples, both in the field and in the laboratory. It is often desirable to collect reliable rock samples from regions of poor and/or insufficient outcrops. These problems are obviously avoided when collecting subsurface samples. These ash-flow sheets are genetically related to large caldera complexes in the central and western San Juan Mountains. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies of Jurassic rocks of South America are of basic importance in defining the beginning of the fragmentation of the South America-Africa block. This was noted by Valencio & Vilas (1969) who, on the basis of the available palaeo- magnetic data, indicated the importance of knowing the Jurassic polar position for South America. These authors started the palaeomagnetic studies of lavas of the Chon-Aike Formation of Middle Jurassic age from Argentina. The first Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole for South America was computed in the study carried out with igneous rocks of this formation from Puerto Deseado, Province of Santa Cruz (4T47' S, 66" W). Vilas (Received 1974 August 2) Summary New palaeomagnetic data for the Middle Jurassic Chon-Aike Formation from 15 different geological units of rhyolitic porphyries, keratophyres, ignimbrites, pumicites and associated tuffs exposed at the Estancia La Reconquista, Province of Santa Cruz (48"10'S, 68"50' W), Argentina, are given. After cleaning, all the units show normally polarized magnetic remanence and the mean of their virtual geomagnetic poles is not coincident with the mean of the virtual geomagnetic poles derived from the Puerto Deseado (Valencio & Vilas) and Camarones (Creer et al.) areas. It is proposed that the most reliable palaeomagnetic pole for the Chon-Aike Formation is that given by the mean of the 54 virtual geomagnetic poles derived from all three areas, namely Puerto Deseado, Camarones and Estancia La Reconquista. It is situated at 85" S, 163" W, with ag5 = 6". rison of the position of this palaeomagnetic pole with the mean of the African Jurassic palaeomagnetic poles suggests that the separation of South America and Africa occurred after the Middle Jurassic. 1. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies of Jurassic rocks of South America are of basic importance in defining the beginning of the fragmentation of the South America-Africa block. This was noted by Valencio & Vilas (1969) who, on the basis of the available palaeo- magnetic data, indicated the importance of knowing the Jurassic polar position for South America. These authors started the palaeomagnetic studies of lavas of the Chon-Aike Formation of Middle Jurassic age from Argentina. The first Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole for South America was computed in the study carried out with igneous rocks of this formation from Puerto Deseado, Province of Santa Cruz (4T47' S, 66" W). Comparison of the position of this pole with those of the Jurassic palaeomagnetic poles for Africa (Briden 1967) suggested that the opening of the South Atlantic occurred before the Middle Jurassic (Valencio & Vilas 1970). Piper (Received 1974 November 4)* Summary Palaeomagnetic results are presented for a variety of Precambrian rocks from south-western Africa. Oldest rocks studied are the Orange River Lavas (> I850 My) from which the three least altered sites give a VGP at 254" E, 19" N near the polar wander curve for Africa at c.2100 My. Five sites from basic intrusions believed to be about 1200 My in age at Ookiep, Namaqualand, give a pole at 155" E, 15" S. Nineteen sites in lavas of the Barby Formation (Sinclair Group, < 1200 My) in South West Africa yield a significant direction after cleaning with five sites reversed with respect to the remainder; grouping is improved after correction for folding (> 1020 My). the predominantly-clastic Kunjas series. Radiometric data suggest a possible age of 1200 My for acid volcanics of the Nagatis Formation (von Brunn 1969). The overlying Sinclair Group is pre- dominantly volcanic and granites intrusive into it but predating the overlying Auborus Formation, include the Rooikam granite dated at 1020+80 My (von Brunn 1969). At the top of the Sinclair Group and separated from it by angular unconformity is a suite of rocks including lava flows and sediments distinguished (Martin 1965) as the Guperas member how considered to be a formation). These lavas were erupted after the bulk of the folding of the Sinclair Group was completed (B. R. Watters 1971, private communication). Folding and intrusion of the Sinclair series was followed by deposition of a thick succession of conglomerates, breccias, red sandstones, and siltstones known as the Auborus formation. In the type area this formation was laid down in a N-S synclinal basin with thick conglomerates at the base and characterized by large lateral changes in lithology and thickness. Sedimentological studies (Miller 1969) suggest deposition under strongly oxidizing conditions with frequent exposure and formation of dessica- tion features. Piper (Received 1974 November 4)* Summary Palaeomagnetic results are presented for a variety of Precambrian rocks from south-western Africa. Oldest rocks studied are the Orange River Lavas (> I850 My) from which the three least altered sites give a VGP at 254" E, 19" N near the polar wander curve for Africa at c.2100 My. Five sites from basic intrusions believed to be about 1200 My in age at Ookiep, Namaqualand, give a pole at 155" E, 15" S. Nineteen sites in lavas of the Barby Formation (Sinclair Group, < 1200 My) in South West Africa yield a significant direction after cleaning with five sites reversed with respect to the remainder; grouping is improved after correction for folding (> 1020 My). Palaeomagnetic results are also given for lavas of the over- lying Guperas Formation (< 1020 h.ly), sediments of the succeeding Auborus Formation, basic dykes at Klein Karas (878+41 My), and six dolerite dykes from Namaqualand (probable age of 653 A- 70 My). Nine sites from the Fish River Formation (probable Lower Cambrian age) give pole positions correlating with a late Precambrian to Ordovician polar shift recognized from other Gon

They are mostly slightly undersaturated and near the junction between andesite and basalt in composition; the bulk are zeolitized. The state of alteration varies from greeschist- amphibolite facies metamorphism (e.g. sites 60-65) where the feldspar and pyroxenes are pseudomorphed by sericite, and chlorite and actinolite respectively, to zeolite- greenschist (e.g. sites 82, 83) in which a primary igneous texture is visible but the pyroxenes and olivines are pseudomorphed, to zeolite facies (e.g. sites 90-93) in which the igneous minerals are entirely fresh. Thus in general degree of alteration diminishes northwards across the sampling area (Fig. 6), and has affected the magnetic minerals to varying degrees. Unoxidized titanomagnetite grains in the more highly altered rocks are surrounded, and sometimes completely pseudomorphed, by altera- tion rims of rutile and haematite; grains also show variable amounts of granulation (Ade-Hall et al. 1968, Part I) within their area. Lavas with an intermediate degree of alteration are at the most marginally granulated and titanomagnetites, generally with oxidation states 1-2, are preserved with slight marginal alteration. Sites 90-93 show an absence of granulation and subdivision by ilmenite lamellae equivalent to oxidation states 2-3, and locally, a pesudomorphing of the ilmenite lamellae gives oxidation states 4 and 5. Sites 66, 68 and 76 are not significant before or after cleaning. When the af cleaned site mean directions are corrected for the local dip of the lavas grouping is considerably improved (Fig. 7, Table 3) and the precision k rises from 2.0 to 4.8 significant at the 95 per cent confidence level using the fold test of McElhinny (1964). Scatter is still larger than would be expected from palaeosecular variation at this palaeolatitude (Irving 1964, page 146) and might be improved if it were possible to correct for plunge components. Furthermore most of the sites are situated within small fault blocks and differential rotation of these blocks may contribute to between-site scatter. Five sites (59, 62, 69 and 93) are magnetized in the opposite sense to the remainder (Table 3) and the first four imply that there are at least two approximate reversals in the lower part of the Barby Series (Fig. 3). Sites 90-93 show an absence of granulation and subdivision by ilmenite lamellae equivalent to oxidation states 2-3, and locally, a pesudomorphing of the ilmenite lamellae gives oxidation states 4 and 5. Site 92 shows two stages of titanomagnetite growth with large, partially resorbed, grains and fine elongated grains in the groundmass and some other sections (e.g. 91 and 93) have fine-grained magnetite pseudomorphing olivine. The volcanic phase which occurred during the deposition of the Upper Series is represented by a thick sequence of tholeiitic dolerites and basalts, reaching a maximum thickness of some 200 m. in the Central High Atlas. A series of continuous flows is interstratified with clays, formed from the erosion of the basalts, and baked red mudstones. The volcanic series has been highly altered and it seems probable that this occurred during or soon after the emplacement of the rocks, as a direct results of extrusion into an aqueous environment. If this is so, then the primary component of magnetic remanence carried by the alteration products should reflect the ambient geomagnetic field direction relative to this region during Middle Triassic times. Introduction Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data from north-west Africa are likely to be of particular use in investigations of the early history of evolution of the central North Atlantic basin, involving separation of eastern North America from north-western Africa. Furthermore, comparison of such data with Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data from south and east Africa would allow us to test the applicability of the geocentric dipole field model to Mesozoic time. For these reasons a palaeomagnetic study has been carried out on Mesozoic formations from the High Atlas and Anti-Atlas regions of Morocco. Reference to such a model is necessary when comparing magnitudes of secular variation from localities of differing latitude. The magnitude of secular variation as measured by the angular dispersion of palaeomagnetic data is latitude dependent, in accord with the latitude dependence of dipole field intensity. Models which attempt to explain this latitude dependence differ only in the relative contributions of a wobbling main dipole field of variable intensity and a westward drifting non-dipole field (Irving gC Ward 1964; Creer, Irving & Nairn 1959; Cox 1962, Cox 1970). Combining the two effects, angular dispersion S, can be written as where S, is the angular dispersion of VGP's produced by the dipole wobble only aild SN is the angular dispersion due to the drifting non-dipole field. Reference to such a model is necessary when comparing magnitudes of secular variation from localities of differing latitude. Studies of palaeosecular variation have not been able to distinguish, at the 95 per cent confidence level (Cox 1969), one model from another, and in most cases model dispersions fall within the estimated confidence limits. The curves for samples 1 and 3 show some characteristic properties of the Kaoko basalt: (i) the Curie points on heating are somewhat higher than 575" C while those measured on cooling are significantly lower, and (ii) the room-temperature saturation magneti- zation is lowered as a result of the heating. These two observations suggest that an initially oxidized titanomagnetite phase breaks down into haematite and another (possibly oxidized) titanomagnetite richer in titanium than the parent phase. Sample 2 has a lower Curie point on heating than samples 1 and 3 but that on cooling is about the same while the room-temperature saturation magnetization after heating is greater than the natural value. Some heating curves show an inflexion oraknee at about 400 "C which disappears on heating at a fixed temperature of 260 "C for a few hours. A possible explanation is that an initial (possibily slightly oxidized) titanium-rich spinel phase becomes more oxidized on heating. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Summary Palaeomagnetic and isotopic results from the Kaoko lavas, Hoachanas basalts and dolerite sills of South-West Africa indicate that the Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic Stormberg flows of South Africa may have extended into SW-Africa and that younger igneous events of Lower Cretaceous age were simultaneous with the Serra Geral volcanism in Brazil. Five analyses on three samples of the Keetmanshoop sills gave K-Ar ages between 17854 and 199k4 Ma, four analyses of two samples of the Hoachanas basalts gave ages between 161 13 and 17352 Ma and eight analyses of five samples of Kaoko basalt gave ages between 110+4 and 12852 Ma. The components of remanent magnetization (RM) used to compute palaeomagnetic pole positions for the Kaoko lavas (48" N, 93" W, A95 = 3") and for the Hoachanas basalts (61" N, 106" W, A95 = 7" are stable to alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization. Correlation on a pre-drift map and on a map reconstructed for 112 Ma BP (before present) between the palaeomagnetic poles from the Kaoko and Serra Geral lavas suggests that the South Atlantic had not opened appreciably by 112 Ma BP. They commonly grade in composition from basic or intermediate at their perimeters to acidic in the cores (Figure 2). The perimeter phase is most commonly diorite, which is often well foliated or gneissic and may have asso- ciated gabbroic zones. Progressing inward, the plutons grade to quartz diorite and then to granodiorite and finally to quartz monzonite in the core. During this gradation the rocks become increasingly massive or less foliated, and hornblende gives way to biotite as the dominant mafic mineral. The petrography and structure of these plutons have been sum- marized by Hutchison [1970]. Of the four plutons sampled in this study, three come from the eastern age zone. The eastern zone yields K-Ar ages of 40-50 m.y., the central zone ages of 64-80 m.y., and the western zone ages of 84-140 m.y. Hutchison [1967] has pointed out that these dates may represent the actual time of emplacement, or the time of regional thermal metamorphic events, or the time at which radiogenic argon ceased to diffuse during gradual uplift and unroofing. Because the paleomagnetic method for determining age from the pole position of a rock unit is less sensitive to thermal updating than the K-Ar method, this study was undertaken as an initial test. The 25 sites (Figure 2) were spread along an 80-km cross- section of the complex to minimize the chance of tectonic rotations, which could move the pole positions and thereby negate the paleomagnetic method. The section follows the Skeena River eastward from Prince Rupert, British Columbia (Figure 2). There are essentially three incompatible hypotheses involving Madagascar. Briefly, one proposal is that Madagascar was once 20 ° north of its present position attached to tire sialic crust of the Seychelles Baak [ 1 ], requiring Madagascar to have a Tanzania-Kenya fit with Africa [2]. In contrast, Dixey [3] suggests that the Mozambique Channel between Africa and Mada- gascar is "geosynclinal" and underlain by Precam- brian granitic crest; Flower and Strong [4] concur, basing their contention on some sandstone inchtsions in some lavas of the Comores Islands. In addition, Madagascar may have occupied the southerly Inham- bane delta region of Mozambique as suggested by Wright arid McCurry [5] and discussed by Strong [6]. Experimental procedures Paleomagnetic cores of 2.5 cm diameter and 10 cm average length were obtained using a portable gasoline- powered drill [13]. The samples were taken a[tnost entirely from coastline ex- posures and roadcuts due to the lack of suitable ex- posures inland. In the laboratory, a 2.3 cm length specimen was cut from the deepest, least-weathered part of each core for paleomagnetic analysis. The renmant mag- netism was measured using a 5 Hz spinner magneto- meter [ 141: unstable magnetic components were mini- mized by application of peak alternating magnetic fields of 100, 200 and 300 Oe to each specimen. The mean magnetic direction was determined using the minimum scatter criterion of Irving, Stott and Ward [15]: this method is discussed by Watkins and Richard- son [16].

movement between plates. The role of Madagascar in Indian Ocean tectonics has proven to be an integral part of all interpretations. There are essentially three incompatible hypotheses involving Madagascar. Briefly, one proposal is that Madagascar was once 20 ° north of its present position attached to tire sialic crust of the Seychelles Baak [ 1 ], requiring Madagascar to have a Tanzania-Kenya fit with Africa [2]. In addition, Madagascar may have occupied the southerly Inham- bane delta region of Mozambique as suggested by Wright arid McCurry [5] and discussed by Strong [6]. Additional constraints must be placed on the tec- tonic interpretations before contrasting hypotheses can be resolved. In the laboratory, a 2.3 cm length specimen was cut from the deepest, least-weathered part of each core for paleomagnetic analysis. The renmant mag- netism was measured using a 5 Hz spinner magneto- meter [ 141: unstable magnetic components were mini- mized by application of peak alternating magnetic fields of 100, 200 and 300 Oe to each specimen. The mean magnetic direction was determined using the minimum scatter criterion of Irving, Stott and Ward [15]: this method is discussed by Watkins and Richard- son [16].
